individual_results.question: What were the main challenges AAC users faced in backchanneling?
individual_results.answer: The main challenges AAC users faced in backchanneling include the lack of a clear way to type short backchanneling utterances or express nuance of these using AAC interfaces, difficulty observing or responding to their conversation partner’s cues due to visual attention focused on the device, and the disruption of the flow of conversation when the backchanneling cue comes too late or when producing a backchanneling utterance interrupts their own message construction.
contexts:
Users of Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) 
technology cannot always rely on instant interjections or effort-
less gestures to engage in backchanneling. These difficulties arise 
because (1) there is no clear way to type short backchanneling 
utterances like “mm-hmm” or express nuance of these using AAC 
interfaces, (2) AAC users often focus their visual attention on the 
device itself, making it hard to observe or respond to their conver-
sation partner’s cues, and (3) the backchanneling cue may come too

versation. Producing a backchanneling utterance can also interrupt 
their own message construction, requiring them to pause typing or 
shift eye focus to tap out a brief response, which can disrupt their 
communication flow. These constraints limit or render traditional 
backchanneling modalities limited or out of sync for AAC users, 
creating barriers to staying actively engaged in conversations.

individual_results.question: How did backchanneling differ in AAC-to-AAC versus AAC-to-non-AAC interactions?

Taken together, these results demonstrate the potential to en-

•the virtual pedestrian should preferentially walk behind the
